answer_text:
Let

\[
B_L=\left\{(x,y): (x-7)^2+(y+3)^2<L^2\right\}.
\]

We want the largest \(L\) such that \(G\) is one-to-one on \(B_L\).

We have

\[
G(x,y)=\bigl((x-1)^2,\;y^4\bigr).
\]

So two points \((x,y)\) and \((x',y')\) map to the same value iff

\[
(x-1)^2=(x'-1)^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
y^4=y'^4.
\]

Thus

\[
x'=x \ \text{or}\ x'=2-x,
\]

and

\[
y'=y \ \text{or}\ y'=-y.
\]

The nontrivial possibilities are the “folds” at \(x=1\) and \(y=0\).

For \(L=3\),

\[
(x-7)^2+(y+3)^2<9
\]

implies

\[
4<x<10
\quad\text{and}\quad
-6<y<0.
\]

On this region:

- \((x-1)^2\) is strictly increasing because \(x>1\);
- \(y^4\) is strictly decreasing because \(y<0\).

Therefore if

\[
G(x,y)=G(x',y')
\]

with both points in the ball of radius \(3\), we must have \(x=x'\) and \(y=y'\). Hence \(G\) is invertible on the neighborhood of radius \(3\). Its local inverse is

\[
x=1+\sqrt{u}, \qquad y=-\sqrt[4]{v}.
\]

Now suppose \(L>3\). Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) such that

\[
0<\varepsilon<L-3.
\]

Then both points

\[
(7,-\varepsilon)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(7,\varepsilon)
\]

lie in the ball centered at \((7,-3)\) of radius \(L\), since

\[
|3-\varepsilon|<L
\quad\text{and}\quad
|3+\varepsilon|<L.
\]

But

\[
G(7,-\varepsilon)=\bigl(36,\varepsilon^4\bigr)
=
G(7,\varepsilon),
\]

so \(G\) is not one-to-one for any \(L>3\).

Therefore the largest possible radius is

\[
\boxed{3}.
\]
